pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A small game studio lives between two deadlines: the publisher milestone that pays the bills, and the launch that has to find players. This workspace keeps the work, the bugs, the playtests and the wishlists in one place so the whole team sees the same picture.
From task to milestone build
Tasks

: every piece of work, tagged by discipline (code, art, animation, audio, design, writing, QA), tied to a milestone with an owner, estimate and due date. Cut tasks stay visible but leave the progress count.
Milestones
: what the publisher has agreed to pay for, with Done means written out, the payment attached, and wishlists at that point. Progress and Open bugs roll up from tasks and bugs.
Bugs
: severity, platform, build, steps to reproduce, the playtest it came from and the milestone it must be fixed by. Mark fixed stamps the day; QA moves it to Verified.
Playtests
: from couch tests to the festival demo, with testers, a fun score, would-buy percentage, wishlist adds and the top findings.
A sprint week
Monday triage (30 minutes): every New bug gets a severity and a milestone; crash and blocker bugs get an owner the same hour.
Each person works from Tasks, My tasks view. Move cards as you go; In review means someone else must look.
Wednesday build: the build number goes on every bug found in it.
Friday: the studio lead reads Progress on the current milestone. Below plan means cutting scope, not adding weekends.
After each playtest, fill in the numbers and top findings within two days and file the bugs from it.

pages.title: Bug triage and the milestone build

text.text: Bugs pile up fastest right before a milestone, which is exactly when the team has the least time. This page is the triage routine and the rules for what blocks a milestone build.
Severity, in our words

cells.text: Fixed before any build leaves the studio
The player cannot continue or loses progress
Clearly wrong and most players will see it
Fixed this milestone if time allows
Wrong but easy to play around
Looks or feels a little off

text.text: Monday triage
Open Bugs, sort New by Reported.
Try to reproduce each one on the platform it was found on. Can't reproduce after two tries: ask the reporter for a clip, leave it New.
Reproduced: set severity, Fix by milestone, and move to Confirmed.
Crash and Blocker: an owner presses Assign to me now and moves it to Fixing.
Won't fix needs a sentence in the bug saying why. Never delete a bug.
Fixing and verifying
The person fixing presses Mark fixed, which stamps the day, and writes the build the fix is in.
Someone else plays the steps in that build and moves it to Verified. The fixer never verifies their own bug.
Milestone build checklist
No Crash or Blocker bugs open against this milestone
Every task in Done means is Done
Build number written on the milestone and in the known issues list
Save files from the last build still load
A full play-through on the slowest target device
Worked example

The closed key test on build 0.4.2 found a cutscene crash and a save loss on handhelds. Both were set to the vertical slice milestone at Monday triage; the crash went to the programmer at once, and the slice build waits until both are Verified.

For an indie game, wishlists before launch are the best early sign of sales, and playtests are how you find out if the game is fun before it is too late to change. This page is how the studio runs a playtest and what it records.
Choose the kind of test

cells.text: Bugs across hardware, early fun score
A big wishlist week alongside many other games

text.text: Running one
Write the one question the test must answer in the playtest plan, for example "Do players find the second hook upgrade?"
Prepare the build, keys and a short survey: fun score from 1 to 10, would you buy it, and two open questions.
During the test, watch at least five people play without helping them.
Within two days, fill in testers, fun score, would buy and wishlist adds, and write the top three findings.
File every bug from the test with Found in playtest set, so the playtest shows Bugs found.
Reading wishlists
Record the wishlist count on each milestone as well, so growth between milestones is visible.
Compare adds per playtest kind on the Dashboard chart; a festival week should far outrun an ordinary week.
A drop in would-buy between two builds matters more than any single score. Read the open answers next to it; they usually name the reason in the players' own words.
Checklist before a public demo
Store page live with capsule art, trailer and five screenshots
Demo ends on a clear call to wishlist
No crash bugs open in the demo build
Survey link shown on the demo's end screen
The board for Monday planning and the daily stand-up. Everything in Next sprint is promised; everything in Backlog is not.
Bugs by severity
A small studio ships by cutting early. Two-week sprints, a hard look at the milestone every Monday, and a rule that a feature is cut before a date slips.
Monday planning (one hour)
Read the milestone's exit criteria aloud. Everything planned has to serve one of them.
Move finished work out of review. Anything In review for more than three days gets a reviewer named now.
Each person pulls tasks to about 80% of their time; the rest is bugs, meetings and surprises.
Crash and Blocker bugs go in first, before any new feature.
The daily stand-up
Ten minutes, standing or on a call: what moved, what is next, what is stuck.
Stuck means someone else has to act. Name them.
Cutting scope

When the milestone's Progress falls behind the calendar (half the time gone, under 40% done), cut. Cutting is a decision, not a failure: move the task to Cut, write one line on why, and tell the publisher in the milestone update.

text.text: Crunch
We do not plan overtime. If the only way to hit a milestone is weekends, cut, or ask the publisher to move the date with the playtest numbers in hand.
